rows.description: A toddler pokes at every new object, asks for the same story with tiny changes, and moves toward unfamiliar sounds and textures. The drive is pure interest; safety still has to come from the adults nearby.

rows.description: A child builds elaborate make-believe worlds, asks endless why questions and tries odd combinations of food or games. Feels excited by novelty and bored by repetition, and needs room to wonder without being called silly.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A child falls into topics like dinosaurs, space or mythology and wants to know everything. Enjoys hypotheticals and strange facts, but may resist rote homework that feels pointless.

rows.description: A teenager questions inherited customs, tries new music, subcultures and philosophies, and enjoys arguing both sides. Feels alive when ideas expand, and may confuse rejecting tradition with independence.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A parent living with a curious, challenging teenager feels unsettled when long-held beliefs are questioned at the dinner table. Both anxiety and pride mix together, and listening first keeps the door open.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: anxiety, curiosity, pride

rows.description: A young adult prefers proven routines, familiar food and clear rules, and feels uneasy when plans keep changing. This is a steady style, not closed-mindedness, and its strength is depth and reliability.

rows.description: A wise young adult notices that the very open and the very traditional both hold value. Asks what the other person's preference protects, and avoids labelling curiosity as shallow or caution as dull.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A colleague notices a friend who keeps switching hobbies, cities and ideas. Some see richness and fresh thinking, others see flakiness; the friend often needs help turning ideas into follow-through.

rows.description: A child lines up shoes, remembers bedtime steps and gets upset when a game is left unfinished. Feels calmer when things have a place, and pride grows when tidy-up is noticed.

rows.description: A child packs the school bag the night before, finishes homework before play and worries about small mistakes. Reliability wins trust from teachers, though rest and play can get squeezed out.
